top_stories.title: Inside the AI Training Data Market — Gabe Greenberg, G2i
top_stories.content: A frontier lab can pay more for training data it gets to keep exclusive, or take a discount on data another lab can buy too. At AI Engineer CODE, G2i founder Gabe Greenberg tells swyx how labs make that decision, how small pilot orders turn into bigger engagements, and when it makes sense to build a data operation in-house. We also get into what the labs are buying. A good training task should sit just ahead of what a model can do today. Gabe explains how senior engineers design the task, choose the starting data, and build a verifier that can score the result. Thanks to G2i for co-organizing AI Engineer CODE 2026 and sponsoring this episode. Join us April 26–27 at AI Engineer Miami 2027. How G2i went from $15M to a projected ~$100M without VC From 6,000-engineer training-data projects to staff-level specialists “If you make them too hard, they become evals” Why a frontier lab can spend a few million dollars just to pilot a data vendor What frontier labs mean when they ask for taste Why picking a data vendor is like picking a barber Why frontier labs sometimes buy the same datasets as their rivals Why idle GPUs push labs to buy training data off the shelf How average handling time (AHT) prices tasks that take a day or two weeks Could a dying startup sell its data? The next training-data markets in CAD, mechanical engineering, and chip design Show notes G2i builds AI training data and reinforcement learning environments with senior engineers. ORC is the multi-agent coding platform Gabe’s team uses internally. Recorded at AI Engineer CODE in San Francisco. items.title: Show HN: DragDropMath – Learn math by feel
items.content: Hi HN!I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious.So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves.I always wanted to make this, but life got in the way. Then a few weeks ago I saw declarative dragging (https://declarative-dragging.github.io/) on the front page of HN and the spark came back!It took quite a few rounds to get the feel right, but I think it's close to what happens in my mind when I mentally manipulate these expressions.A few more points: - There are no ads, no trackers, no accounts (it's a static website and progress is saved in the browser cache). - Teachers can create their own problem sets, encoded in the link. - I plan to add more chapters (trigonometry, complex numbers, some calculus) but I first need to figure out the 'right' mode of interaction. - I just started working on the experience from mobile, so there may still be some rough edges thereI'm curious to know what you think, if you have suggestions for content, if you spot anything that I should fix, if you have feature requests! Thank you in advance

items.title: Android’s DIY widgets are a bit of vibe-coding fun
items.content: Widgets, your way. | Photo: Allison Johnson / The Verge Aside from dealing with my calendar, there's one thing I want AI to do: tell me if I'm about to miss the bus. What I need is a widget. It needs to tell me real-time arrivals for the bus stop near my house. Tapping around on my phone screen to open the right app and select my stop will slow me down enough to miss a bus. I need glanceable information, and I hoped that Android's vibe-coded widget feature could help me out here. It hasn't, to my disappointment, but I still had a good time cooking up other widgets. items.title: datasette-charts 0.4a0
items.content: Release: datasette-charts 0.4a0 The new datasette-charts plugin has its own plugin hook to allow other plugins to define new chart types, but I hadn't actually used it for anything yet. I had Claude Opus 5.5 build an experimental plugins just to try out the hook and it came up with a bunch of friction points in the design. This release addresses those, which should make building additional chart plugins a whole lot more ergonomic. I've also added a website for the plugin, at charts.datasette.io. The new website includes a tutorial for plugin authors, and a gallery showing all of the core charts and annotations, each one linking to an interactive demo on Datasette Lite. Tags: datasette-charts, datasette, visualization, datasette-lite
